newsitem.title: UK: Ldn gold marks time while PGMs lose their lustre.
newsitem.headline: Ldn gold marks time while PGMs lose their lustre.

text.p: Fresh Russian assertions that long-delayed platinum and palladium exports will resume this month sent prices on the white metals lower early on Tuesday, dealers said.
And gold and silver languished in slow trading at the bottom end of recent price ranges amid bearish market sentiment.
Gold was fixed $341.40 an ounce, just $0.10 lower than the Monday afternoon fixing. Silver was similarly sluggish, last indicated at an unchanged $4.71/$4.73.
"Gold and silver are feeling a bit bearish, yet people are still nervous to go short here at the bottom end of the range," a dealer said, pegging gold's broader range at $339-$348.

Trading activity was muted with many market operators attending the Financial Times Gold Conference in Prague. But the market was watching currency gyrations for clues to gold's next move, dealers said.
The softening Australian dollar was seen encouraging producers to sell their output forward as the price of gold denominated in the domestic currency grows.
The platinum group metals (PGMs) came lower in early European trading following a Tass report which cited a senior Norilsk Nickel official saying Russian exports would resume in June.
Russian supplies have been blocked since the start of 1997, leading to extreme supply tightness in the market and a frantic price rally earlier this month .
Platinum was last quoted $11 lower at $415.00/420.00, after starting to come off late on Monday amid New York-based long liquidation and switching out of the July contract.
Strong support was expected at the psychological $400 level.
Palladium's decline was more muted as the market is still very tight, but prices were off $7 at $194.00/$199.00.

"We saw some nervous two-way interest this morning as news came of yet another statement of a return to normal of Russian shipments," a dealer said. But he noted that Russian officials already had said earlier this month that supplies should resume soon.
"The picture is larger now than simply Russian supplies. Fund interest holds the key," the dealer said.
The U.S. fund Tiger Management, which is believed to have stockpiled 1.5 million ounces of palladium, is seen partly responsible for rare metal's recent spike to 17-year highs.
Traders said Tiger fund official had visited Japan last week to persuade Japanese trade houses to buy supplies from the fund.
